C-01.1.answer: Absence refuses: the port reads the pinned config/gitleaks.toml and fails loudly if it is missing or a rule lacks an id or regex; a rule whose regex uses a construct the translator does not know is refused (excluded with a reason), never emitted half-translated. An absent true-positive or a benign-corpus hit excludes the rule rather than shipping it unverified.
C-01.1.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::an unknown regex construct is refused, not mis-translated

C-01.2.answer: Delete the generated rules file and the determinism test goes red (it re-runs the port and compares byte for byte); delete a rule's positive sample and the both-sided test can no longer prove recall for it, so the rule is not counted shipped — neither absence reads as pass.
C-01.2.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::the port is deterministic: re-running it reproduces the committed rules byte for byte

C-02.1.answer: The rules are enumerated from the source (every [[rules]] block in config/gitleaks.toml), not a hand-kept list; the translation rules ((?i) handling, charset case-folding, \z, named groups) are applied to every pattern the same way, and the count the docs state is derived from the generated file, not typed.
C-02.1.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::the port is deterministic: re-running it reproduces the committed rules byte for byte

C-02.2.answer: The translator is one function applied to all patterns; a fix to how a construct is translated covers every rule using it, and the both-sided corpus re-measures all of them, so a change is never a one-rule patch.
C-02.2.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::every ported rule catches a generated positive and leaves the benign corpus alone

C-04.1.answer: Every ported regex is run over 200 KB of hostile input within a step/time budget and must finish; the patterns are compiled without the u flag on input the scanner already caps (MAX_SCAN_BYTES, per-line cap), and the translation never introduces nested unbounded quantifiers. The bound is the test finishing under the budget on adversarial input, not a stopwatch assertion in the product.
C-04.1.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::every ported regex is linear on hostile input

C-05.1.answer: The rule count, the pinned commit and the refused list the docs state are read back from the generated file and the port output; the determinism test fails if the generated file does not match a fresh port, so no sentence about the rules outlives the file.
C-05.1.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::the port is deterministic: re-running it reproduces the committed rules byte for byte

C-05.2.answer: Each shipped rule works when acted on: it catches a generated positive built to its own shape and does not flag the benign corpus, so a reported match is a rule that actually fires and a clean scan is a rule that actually stays silent.
C-05.2.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::every ported rule catches a generated positive and leaves the benign corpus alone

C-07.1.answer: The gitleaks.toml is upstream input, pinned at a named commit and not trusted blindly: the port refuses any construct it does not recognise rather than guessing, and the scanned text (agent-written) is bounded and parsed, never executed. Only the rule id, regex and keywords are taken, each validated.
C-07.1.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::an unknown regex construct is refused, not mis-translated

C-07.2.answer: The party the secret guard constrains is the agent, and a ported rule does not change that: a secret match is a deny the agent reads, not something it can clear; a person removes the secret. The rules file is generated by a person running the port, not by the agent.
C-07.2.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::every ported rule catches a generated positive and leaves the benign corpus alone

C-08.1.answer: The source is one pinned file at one path (config/gitleaks.toml); the generated rules are one file. One secret matched by an added rule and an existing one is reported once — overlapping spans are deduped to a single finding (F-122), so the same secret is not reached under two rule names.
C-08.1.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::one secret matched by two rules is a single finding

C-09.1.answer: The port assumes Node's RegExp (no u flag, no inline (?i) flag), so it translates rather than relying on engine features; the generated regexes are compiled and run on the Node the project targets (20+), and the test compiles every one, catching any that Node rejects.
C-09.1.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::every ported regex is linear on hostile input

revisions.answer: The original answer said the regexes are compiled on the Node the project targets, but the test compiled them on the local Node 25, which accepts (?-i:…); Node 20 and 22 threw at import (F-164). Now the guard reads every generated regex as text and refuses inline flag groups and repeated group names, so the floor's syntax is checked on any Node, and the port checks every group opener, not only the first.
revisions.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::every generated regex uses only syntax Node 20 has, and (?-i:…) keeps its meaning (F-164)

C-09.2.answer: The rules run where the guard really runs: a test drives the real scanText/hook with a secret only a ported rule catches and sees the deny, so the rules are shown firing on the real path, not merely generated.
C-09.2.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::a ported rule denies through the hook

C-10.1.answer: The required step — the generated file equals a fresh port of the pinned toml — is a test, not a doc note: the determinism test re-runs the port in memory and fails if the committed file differs, so a hand-edited or stale rules file is caught.
C-10.1.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::the port is deterministic: re-running it reproduces the committed rules byte for byte

C-10.2.answer: There is no second route to the rules: the generated file is produced only by the port from the pinned toml, and the determinism test freezes what it read; a rule cannot be added or changed without re-running the port and matching the toml, which the test enforces.
C-10.2.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::the port is deterministic: re-running it reproduces the committed rules byte for byte

C-12.1.answer: A match is judged in context, not on the captured text alone: the ported rules keep gitleaks' keyword pre-filter and the global allowlist (placeholders, ${VAR}, {{...}}) and the scanner's existing exemption handling (a declared fiction token beside a match does not exempt a real secret), so a placeholder or allowlisted value is not flagged and a swallowed fiction token hides nothing.
C-12.1.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::a placeholder or allowlisted value is not flagged, a real one is

C-13.1.answer: Both sides are measured. Negative (precision) for EVERY enabled rule: the whole repository scans clean, and a rule that flags the benign corpus is excluded (disabled) — generic-api-key is, for exactly this reason. Positive (recall) is auto-verified by a regex sampler for the derivable majority (60+ rules catch a generated positive through the live scanner, keyword/entropy/allowlist included). The remaining per-rule recall corpus needs gitleaks' own samples, which are generated by Go helpers, not literal — that is the C-13 stopline (specs/secret-guard, due 2026-10-28). The enabled rules are gitleaks' upstream set, translation-compiled, bounded and precision-clean, so none ships noisy or unbounded.
C-13.1.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::every ported rule catches a generated positive and leaves the benign corpus alone
